title: Doctor's waiting room
hook: Julian of Norwich, sick enough to think she'd die, hears that all shall be well
tomorrow: what did Epictetus say to do when the ship hits a storm?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thoreau's Holy-Lander: saunter, a walk as a small pilgrimage. Today the walk ends in a room with plastic chairs and a clipboard.

A TV on mute, a clipboard on your knee, a name called that isn't yours. The waiting room is where a mind runs to the worst case. Julian of Norwich knew a version of that room. In her book, Revelations of Divine Love, she tells how she lay so sick that she and those around her believed she would die. Her curate came and set a cross before her face. In that illness she received what she called showings. Among the words she heard were these: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well."
screen: `A NAME THAT ISN'T YOURS.` → `JULIAN, SO SICK.` → `A CROSS BEFORE HER FACE.` → `ALL SHALL BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Julian heard that line while asking about the hardest thing she knew: why there is sin and pain at all. It isn't a promise that the scan comes back clear. Julian's teaching, as a Christian mystic, is that God's love holds everything, including what goes wrong, and that in the end nothing falls outside it. So in her reading, the line doesn't say nothing bad will happen. It says whatever happens won't fall outside love. Some borrow her words for a wait like this. And the shape of the line helps: it doesn't ask you to know the result first. That's a different job from googling. Googling tries to know the future early. Julian's line lets you not know yet. She didn't get a forecast either. What she reports receiving was a promise about love, big enough to hold whatever the forecast turns out to be.
screen: `SHE ASKED ABOUT SIN AND PAIN.` · `NOT A PROMISE OF A CLEAR SCAN.` · `NOTHING FALLS OUTSIDE LOVE.` · `HELD, WITHOUT KNOWING YET.` · then, large: `WAITING.`

segments.voice: Sit as you would in a waiting-room chair: feet flat, hands on your knees. Breathe in slowly, then breathe out a little longer than you breathed in. If you pray, you can borrow Julian's words on the out-breath; if you don't, let the long out-breath be enough.
Doctor's waiting room: the chair where you don't know yet. Julian's line holds the not knowing: all shall be well.
The line to keep: waiting, held while you don't know yet. Seven of fourteen, the halfway chair.

screen: `DAY 1762 COUNTS.` → `ORDINARY DAYS · 7 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID EPICTETUS SAY TO DO IN A STORM AT SEA?`

howItsDone: Christians who read Julian of Norwich repeat 'all shall be well' in hard waits; people on this path borrow the shape, breathing slowly and letting the not knowing be held.
